WAWI-NO · Oslo · Investment memo

Wallenius Wilhelmsen (WAWI-NO): the peak earnings are under contract, but the shares already pay a peak multiple, so the expected return is the dividend less the decline in forward earnings

15 November 2026. Money in USD millions unless stated; per-share figures in USD. Share price NOK 163.2 (9 November 2026), about USD 17.0 at USD/NOK 9.6. EPS is after the 20% minority in EUKOR Car Carriers; the bases and sources are in the end notes.

Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in one line

Wallenius Wilhelmsen is turning the tightest car-carrier market on record into three years of contracted earnings, and the share price already pays for those earnings: the shares offer peak earnings on a peak multiple, with the unusual and valuable feature that the peak earnings are under contract.

What to do today

At NOK 163 the stock fails Richard’s test, but it is worth keeping close. The case is one of delivery without surprise, so it lacks the unusually positive skew of outcomes and upgrades that would justify a position. The skew would turn positive if the car-carrier sector de-rated on a Suez or China headline while the 17 February 2027 report confirmed the contracts: at the guideline multiple, an entry price of about NOK 125–135, about a fifth below today’s price, would give about 10% a year over 18 months.

Dividend yield~8%a year: the only positive part of the return
What the price assumes7× USD 1.4bn"normal" EBITDA, doubled in 21 months
The date that narrows the cone17 Feb 2027confirmation, not surprise
  1. The contract calendar sets the earnings; the car-carrier cycle sets the share price. 41% of the shipping contract book reprices for 2027, which lifts EBITDA by about 14% and EPS by about 20%. Contracts then hold 2028 earnings. The give-back comes in 2029–2030, when the three-year contracts being signed now and the contract with Hyundai Motor Group (HMG), a quarter of volume, expire together. The contracts make earnings forecastable to within about 10%, but they do not make the share price forecastable: the share price moves with the car-carrier trade, not with the company’s earnings.
  2. EPS rises from USD 1.58 in 2026 to 1.90 in 2027, then declines to 1.76, 1.65 and 1.52 by 2030. The forecast contains one year of double-digit growth followed by a gentle decline. 2027 EBITDA comes back to within 4% of the 2024 record, but 2027 EPS stays 18% below its record, because depreciation on the renewed fleet, the HMG minority and 4% more shares take more of each dollar of EBITDA.
  3. Estimates leave no room for an upgrade skew. Guidance holds no cushion. Consensus 2027 EBITDA already equals my forecast, and consensus 2027 EPS sits about 5% above mine. My 2028 forecast is 5% above consensus on EBITDA and level on EPS. The steep upgrades are behind the stock.
  4. The share price is really pricing the 2030s. Today’s price equals about seven times a “normal” EBITDA of USD 1.4bn, and the leading broker has doubled its normal-EBITDA assumption in 21 months. No company report in the next 18 months can confirm a normal EBITDA of USD 1.4bn.
  5. The expected return is the dividend less the decline in forward earnings. A dividend yield of about 8% a year is real and affordable. Against the yield, the two-year-forward earnings that the market values roll from 2028 into 2029–2030, and the starting multiple is above the guideline fair multiple. The model’s return at the guideline fair multiple is −0.8% over 18 months and −3.2% over three years; like for like, on EPS after the minority, the return is about −12% and −10%.
  6. One date narrows the range of outcomes: 17 February 2027. The fourth-quarter report will give the contract book’s average rate, the backlog and the first 2027 guidance. The report’s value lies in confirmation, not surprise.
  7. Four developments would turn the skew positive: a share price about a fifth lower with the contracts confirmed; a book average rate of USD 60 per cubic metre (cbm) or more in February; cancellation of the US port fees; or car carriers staying out of the Suez Canal through 2028.

The five judgements that move the value most (arithmetic in #9):

J1

J1. The price won on the 41% of the book renewing for 2027. I assume a rise of about USD 15 per cbm. Each USD 5 per cbm is USD 0.18 of 2027 EPS.

J2

J2. Whether customers ship the volumes they have contracted through the gap in Chinese exports that should follow the current pull-forward. Each 1% of volume is USD 0.05 of 2027 EPS.

J3

J3. Whether US port fees return, and who pays them. A full year of fees, half recovered from customers, costs USD 0.31 of 2027 EPS.

J4

J4. Where the book reprices in 2030, and therefore what “normal” earnings are. Each USD 5 per cbm is USD 0.35 of 2030 EPS; each USD 100m of normal EBITDA is about NOK 15 a share.

J5

J5. How much EBITDA reaches shareholders after finance cost, the minority, lease cash and the payout ratio. USD 25m of finance cost is USD 0.05 of EPS; ten points of payout ratio is about one point of yield.

1Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the absence of headwinds

The car-carrier market is the tightest on record, but it reaches Wallenius Wilhelmsen’s earnings only through contracts, and the headwinds are dated and clustered in the next six months.

Evidence: the tailwinds.

  • Demand growth is a push from one country, China. Chinese vehicle exports are up about 50% in 2026 to roughly 10m units, a quarter of world vehicle trade against 1% a decade ago, and they travel long distances. End demand is weak: Chinese domestic registrations are down more than 20% and global light-vehicle sales are down 4%. Chinese factories are exporting a surplus.
  • Capacity is as tight as it has ever been. Fleet utilisation is 96–98%. A one-year charter for a ship of 6,500 car equivalent units (CEU) costs about USD 95–100k a day, more than double the late-2025 trough. Shippers moved 1.0–1.5m cars in containers in the first half of 2026, more than 70 car carriers’ worth of cargo, against about 50 new car carriers delivering in 2027. Routing around the Cape of Good Hope absorbs about 5% of fleet capacity, and port congestion absorbs 18%.

Evidence: the headwinds, which are dated.

  • 1 December 2026: the EU caps imports of Chinese hybrids at 350k a year, against a run-rate of about 900k.
  • 9 January 2027: the suspension of US port fees expires; lawyers expect rolling extensions of two to three months.
  • 1 April 2027: China cuts its export VAT rebate on new-energy vehicles (NEVs) from 13% to 9%.
  • Through 2027–2028: the car-carrier fleet grows 6.6% and then 3.6%. Ordering has restarted (the orderbook rose from 21% of the fleet in March 2026 to 27% in October 2026), and no car carriers were scrapped in 2024–2025.
  • Undated: car carriers returning to the Suez Canal.
  • Already visible: shipments are being pulled forward ahead of the December and April deadlines. China’s passenger-car association expects export growth to slow to about 10% in 2027, and the shipping-data firm Esgian reported in October that the market “shows signs of peaking”.
  • Not sold out outside Asia: the company’s third-quarter volume fell 3% on the second quarter, and high-and-heavy cargo (machinery, 26% of volume and the best-paying cargo) is slowing.

Inference: three consequences follow.

1

The demand driver is real but set by policy, and nobody can forecast it: the leading broker moved its forecast of 2027 Chinese export growth from +1% to double digits in three months.

2

The market reaches the company through contracts, with a lag and, at first, with the opposite sign. The tight market arrived first as higher cost: 2026 EBITDA falls 12% while charter rates double. The tight market arrives as higher price only in 2027. The same lag will apply on the way down.

3

The operating environment therefore now matters for only two things: the market in which the 2029–2030 renewals will be signed, and the valuation multiple of the shares.

So what

The tailwind to 2027 earnings is already banked by contract. The tailwind’s effect on the share price is still fully live, in both directions.

Where I differ from the market. The prevailing narrative calls the Chinese export boom structural, with growth of 10–15% a year to 2029. I agree on the direction (Chinese makers’ share of European car sales is rising from 5% to 12%) and disagree on the reliability. Autos analysts discuss the pull-forward and the gap that should follow it; shipping analysts do not. Shipping investors therefore probably under-weight the risk of weak volumes in the first half of 2027.

Strongest counter-case. Car-carrier supply may limit itself. Shipyards are full until 2030, and 59% of the fleet was built in 2011 or earlier and faces tightening carbon rules, so the market could re-tighten in 2029–2030, exactly when the company’s book reprices. Trade barriers may also redirect cars onto longer routes (to Britain, Latin America and South-East Asia) and so raise tonne-miles.

Watch

What would change my view. Chinese exports holding near 0.8m vehicles a month through April to June 2027; no car carriers back in the Suez Canal by the end of 2027; the first scrapping of car carriers; idle tonnage staying near 2% of the fleet.

Conclusion: the tailwinds are strong but at their peak rate, and the headwinds are not absent: they are dated, clustered in the next six months, and aimed at the share’s multiple and the 2029–2030 renewals more than at 2027 earnings.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. The tightest car-carrier market on record (96-98% utilisation, charter rates doubled, Chinese exports +50%) reaches the company only through contracts, adding a one-off price step to 2027 revenue and margin, but demand is a policy-set push from one country with dated offsets (EU hybrid cap, VAT rebate cut, pull-forward gap) and fleet growth of 6.6% then 3.6% on a 27% orderbook, so over two to three years the net external force is a mild positive that fades by 2029; I agree with the group's 54 and place it below Instalco's turning end-market and above Tenaris's mixed one.

2Internally driven corporate change, and the absence of problems

Management is banking the peak well, but its changes raise the floor under earnings rather than lift earnings above the cycle, and the equity raise shows that problems are not absent.

Evidence: what management is changing.

  • Locking in the peak. The company has won USD 1.7bn of three-year contract awards since the third quarter and expects “the vast majority” of 2027–2029 capacity to be contracted by year-end; management describes the system as “pretty much sold out” for those years.
  • Renewing the fleet cheaply. Two of the 14 Shaper-class ships have been delivered and 11 are financed; all 14 were ordered before shipyard prices rose. The Shapers are the largest car carriers ever built and burn about 25% less fuel per unit carried. The Shapers replace chartered ships rather than add capacity: lease liabilities fell from USD 1,538m to 1,459m in nine months. The company also holds twelve purchase options on chartered ships to 2031, and it has just exercised one about USD 50m below market value.
  • Lifting logistics. The cash EBITDA margin of the logistics business has risen from 2% in 2025 to 7.6%, against a target of 10% for 2028.
  • Tightening the financial frame. The return-on-capital target rose from 8% to 12%; the leverage cap fell to below 3.0 times; a USD 1bn liquidity floor was set; and the EUKOR put and call options were deferred to 2031.

Evidence: what jars.

  • The 2026 guidance was cut in May, in a booming market, because of costs.
  • Liquidity ran down to the USD 1bn floor, and the company raised USD 300m of equity one month after paying a USD 258m dividend.
  • The company ordered four new ships for 2030–2031, with options on eight more, at shipyard prices 20% above the long-run average.
  • The Chief Customer Officer changed on 1 November 2026, in the middle of the largest contract-renewal round in a decade. The logistics business has an interim head. Digital leadership turned over twice in 2025, and the digital programme cost USD 12m of one-off charges in the third quarter alone.

Inference. The internal changes amount to good stewardship of a cyclical peak, not a transformation. Strategy and leadership are continuous, there is no M&A, and the company’s perimeter barely moves. The changes do two useful things: they convert a cyclical peak into contracted cash, and they lower unit cost, so the floor under earnings is higher than in the 2010s. The changes do not lift earnings above the 2023–2025 level, because the identifiable self-help (about USD 95–120m by 2028) roughly offsets cost inflation of about USD 40m a year.

→
So what

Internal change makes the downside shallower and the dividend more durable. Internal change does not create a second leg of earnings growth.

Where I differ from the market. The leading broker forecasts 2028 EBITDA above 2027 partly on “efficiencies”. I think the efficiencies are real but are largely in the 2026 run-rate already (logistics) or shared with customers through the fuel surcharge (the Shapers’ fuel savings).

Strongest counter-case. The company sells contract duration as well as price: its book averages USD 54 per cbm against USD 82 at Höegh Autoliners. One reading is that the company has left money on the table. The better reading late in a cycle is the opposite: duration is what an owner should sell at the top, and the gap between USD 54 and USD 82 is the opportunity the company is now collecting through its renewals.

Watch

What would change my view. Logistics EBITDA reaching USD 50m a quarter; savings in sales, general and administrative costs (SG&A) showing net of restructuring costs; or, negatively, the eight options on Jinling-built ships declared alongside another equity issue.

Conclusion: the internal changes are sound, well funded and aimed at banking the peak; they raise the floor and protect the dividend, but they are not strong enough to carry earnings past the cycle, and the equity raise and peak-priced ship orders show that problems are not absent.

Score: 54, set by the Rater. Management is banking the peak well (USD 1.7bn of three-year awards, cheaply ordered Shapers replacing charters, logistics margin from 2% to 7.6%, a 12% return target), but the self-help of USD 95-120m only offsets cost inflation and creates no second leg, while a guidance cut in a boom, a USD 300m equity raise a month after a USD 258m dividend, peak-priced ship orders and turnover in commercial and logistics leadership show problems are present; this is gently positive stewardship, close to the group's 55, below ASML's partly internal story and just above Reply's continuity.

3Industry structure, competitive advantage, financial profile and management

The foundations are sound but not exceptional: integration buys a softer downturn, not a higher peak, and pricing power comes from scarcity rather than from industry structure.

Evidence.

Structure. The company is number one or two by capacity, with 16.1% of the fleet; the top five operators hold 64%. Entry needs 40–50 ships, terminal access and shipyard slots that do not exist before 2030. But the industry has no exit, and the new capacity belongs to the owners least likely to price for a return: Chinese state and car-maker fleets (about 10% of the fleet including orders) and Hyundai Glovis, which adds 20% to its capacity in 2027.
Advantage. The company owns eight terminals and about 70 vehicle-processing centres; 70% of its top 50 customers buy both ocean and land services; and its customer relationships last decades. Pricing power is real, but it comes from the scarcity of ships, not from the structure of the industry.
Financial profile. Return on capital employed is 15.6% against the 12% target, cash conversion is about 95% of EBITDA, leverage is 1.3 times and the tax rate is about 5%. Against that, the pure-play peer earns more on every measure (EBITDA margin 44% against 34%; return on invested capital 26% against 18%), and over 2010–2019 the company’s returns were below its cost of capital (4.7% in 2019).
Management. The chief executive, in post since 2022, is a plain-spoken operator who has halved debt, sold a non-core terminal at a good price, declined bad renewals and cut guidance promptly. He has not yet been tested by a downturn in this role, and he owns few shares. Two families control about three quarters of the shares and want dividends. HMG is at once the largest customer, a 20% co-owner of EUKOR and the owner of a rival carrier.

The pure-play peer earns more on every measure: integration buys a softer downturn, not a higher peak.

Inference. Wallenius Wilhelmsen is a good franchise in an industry structure that is generous when capacity is tight and unforgiving when capacity is loose. Integration buys stickiness and a softer downturn, not a higher peak: the smaller pure-play peer’s higher margins prove the point. Management quality supports confidence in execution; it is not a reason to expect the company to beat the cycle.

Shipping earns most of the revenue (USD 3.9bn of 5.2bn in 2025), so the franchise rises and falls with the car-carrier cycle.

So what

The foundations justify assuming that contracts are honoured, customers are kept and the balance sheet never becomes the problem. The foundations do not justify capitalising peak margins.

Where I differ from the market. The bull narrative treats the integrated model and the green fleet as reasons for a structurally higher “normal” level of earnings. I treat them as reasons for a higher floor. The difference between the two readings is worth several hundred million dollars of assumed normal EBITDA (J4).

Strongest counter-case. The industry may now be better than its history: there are half as many active shipyards as in 2008, carbon rules are retiring old ships, and customers are signing five-year contracts for the first time. If those changes hold, the 2010s are the wrong reference for normal returns.

Watch

What would change my view. Rivals scrapping ships instead of ordering them; Chinese customers honouring multi-year contracts through a soft patch; the company’s margins converging on the pure-play peer’s as the Shapers arrive.

Conclusion: a favourable industry structure today and a mid-ranking, cyclical franchise through the cycle, run by a competent and honest team whose owners prefer payouts: sound foundations, not exceptional ones.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. A top-two position in a concentrated industry with terminals, processing centres and sticky integrated customers, run by a competent, honest operator, but pricing power comes from scarcity not structure, there is no exit and the new capacity belongs to state and OEM fleets, and through the cycle returns were below the cost of capital (4.7% in 2019) with the pure-play peer earning more; today's ROIC of 17.6% (percentile 87) and EBITDA margin (percentile 84) are a cyclical peak, not the through-cycle truth, and new ships are now ordered at yard prices 20% above average, so I sit it in the middle of the groups (48-56), just below Shell's cycle-bound quality and above Xvivo.

4Conservatism of guidance and the record of delivery

Guidance is honest, current-year only and without a cushion, so any positive surprise in 2027 must come from facts (the renewal price, port fees, volume), not from stored-up conservatism.

Evidence.

  • What is guided. The company guides one figure, for the current year only: 2026 adjusted EBITDA of “about USD 1.6bn”. The first nine months delivered USD 1,178m, so the fourth quarter needs about 422m against 428m in the third quarter.
  • The record. First guidance proved too high in two of the last three years (panel below), and the record available shows no guidance raise within a year under this chief executive.
  • Below EBITDA. Net profit missed consensus by 4% and 8% in the last two quarters, while EBITDA landed within 5% of consensus.
  • What “adjusted” leaves out. Adjusted EBITDA excludes digital and restructuring costs every quarter, and it excluded port fees in 2025. Reported EBITDA for the first nine months of 2026 is USD 1,144m, 3% below the adjusted figure.
  • Expectations management. Management steers expectations in neither direction. In September the company disclosed for the first time that its book averages USD 54 per cbm, in a market where peers sign above USD 100. The disclosure invites the sell-side to pencil in the gap, and nothing in management’s conduct restrains that reading.

The record is “meets EBITDA, misses a little below it”: first guidance proved too high in two of the last three years.

First guidance has proved too high in two of the last three years, each time because of a cost he did not foresee. The estimate upgrades of the past year came from the cycle and from one broker’s change of view, not from a company keeping the bar low.

So what

A positive surprise cannot come from stored-up conservatism. A positive surprise has to come from facts: the renewal price, port fees and volume.

Where I differ from the market. Investors are reading management’s confident words (“rates closely reflecting current strong market conditions”) as upside to the numbers. The record says to read those words as an honest description that will turn into a guidance range close to where estimates already sit. I expect the first 2027 range to be about USD 100m wide and centred on USD 1.80–1.85bn.

Strongest counter-case. Guidance may be conservative by omission: the company guides nothing for 2027–2029, when the input forces are the strongest since 2022, and the second-half 2026 run-rate of EBITDA is already USD 1.70bn a year.

Watch

What would change my view. A first 2027 range centred above USD 1.85bn, or a first-quarter report in May 2027 that holds guidance through the fuel-cost lag and the January port-fee date. The 2026 guidance cut came at the equivalent report in May 2026.

→

Conclusion: guidance is honest, current-year only and without a cushion; the delivery record is “meets EBITDA, misses a little below it”, and management has no habit of raising guidance or of holding expectations down.

Score: 40, set by the Rater. Only current-year EBITDA is guided, 2025 finished 5% below the initial aim after withdrawal and 2026 was cut in May and tracks 6% below the first midpoint, with no raise under this chief executive, net profit missing consensus by 4% and 8% in the last two quarters and no effort to restrain a sell-side reading the USD 54 book rate as upside; the misses are small and EBITDA meets the cut guide, so it sits between the groups' 47 and 34, below Instalco's one-year target miss and above Hexatronic's longer run of walk-backs.

5Pricing power, operating and financial leverage, cost scope and feedback loops

High fixed costs turn 5.5% revenue growth into 20% EPS growth in 2027, but the same gearing then works mildly in reverse, so EPS, not EBITDA, is the line to watch.

Evidence and mechanics.

  • Pricing power is cyclical and released by the contract calendar. In a normal year 20–30% of the book renews. In 2026, 41% renews for 2027. The HMG block does not renew until 2030.
  • Operating leverage is high, and half of it sits below EBITDA. About USD 850–870m of depreciation and finance cost is fixed (the rule in the box below converts EBITDA into EPS). The same cost structure took EBITDA from USD 571m in 2019 to 1,901m in 2024 on revenue up 77%.
  • Higher prices have not reached profit lately. In 2024–2025 only 35–50% of rate gains reached EBITDA, because lower volume, the fuel-cost lag, short-term charters and port fees absorbed the rest. The forecast needs about 70% of rate gains to reach EBITDA in 2027. The third quarter of 2026 showed that such conversion can happen once costs stop rising: Shipping EBITDA rose 19% on the quarter.
  • Financial leverage is low. Interest is about 8% of EBITDA and 70% hedged, so debt adds little gearing and little risk.
  • Cost scope is defensive. In an upturn, cost savings only offset inflation (#2). In a downturn, the 2020 playbook (USD 210m of savings, charters returned to owners, ships laid up) is available.
The rule to carry
EPS ≈ (EBITDA − 860) ÷ 510
USD 100m of EBITDA = USD 0.20 a share1% of EBITDA ≈ 1.9% of EPS

The feedback loops that matter.

Reinforcing1

Scarcity lengthens contracts (reinforcing to 2029, then a cliff). Customers pay for security of capacity, so the company locks in the peak, and its re-exposure to market rates is concentrated at the end of 2029.

Balancing2

High rates bring new ship orders (balancing, with a delay). The orderbook has rebounded, and both listed car carriers raised equity within six weeks of each other, at NOK 167 and 168 a share, to buy ships.

Balancing3

Zero scrapping stores capacity (balancing, then reversing). Old ships kept in service today will leave the fleet as carbon rules bite from 2028–2030.

Pro-cyclical4

The family-dividend loop (pro-cyclical). High payouts at the top of the cycle ran cash down to the liquidity floor and forced the equity raise.

Liability5

The EUKOR loop. The EUKOR put and call options from 2031 are priced on EUKOR’s profits in the preceding three years. The more EUKOR earns in 2028–2030, the more the company may owe HMG (a liability carried at about USD 0.4–0.5bn), in the same year that the company’s contracts reprice.

Inference. Revenue growth produced outsized profit growth in 2020–2024, when price and utilisation rose together. From here the lever is price alone on a capped volume base, pulled one contract tranche at a time. In 2027 the price lever turns 5.5% revenue growth into 14% EBITDA growth and 20% EPS growth. After 2027 the same gearing works gently in reverse, and the costs below EBITDA work against the shareholder throughout.

→
So what

EBITDA is the wrong line to watch. The 2027 step is real, but from 2028 each 1% of EBITDA lost costs nearly 2% of EPS.

Where I differ from the market. The market values the company on a multiple of EBITDA, which ignores lease principal of USD 350–430m a year, the HMG minority and the new shares. EBITDA flatters the equity; EPS and equity free cash flow do not.

Strongest counter-case. Shaper deliveries shrink the lease book and cut fuel and charter costs, so the conversion of EBITDA into cash improves each year to 2029. I agree, and the improving conversion is why free cash flow inflects in 2028 (#6).

Watch

What would change my view. Two consecutive quarters in 2027 in which at least 70% of the price element in the company’s freight-rate bridge reaches EBITDA.

Conclusion: the business has real pricing power and high gearing, but for the next four years the gearing delivers one year of outsized profit growth and then runs mildly backwards, with the costs below EBITDA taking a larger share than the market’s EBITDA lens shows.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. The structure has real fixed-cost gearing (about USD 860m of depreciation and finance cost fixed, each 1% of EBITDA about 1.9% of EPS, EBITDA from 571 to 1,901 on revenue +77% in 2019-2024) and a 2020 cost-out playbook, but pricing power is cyclical scarcity released one contract tranche at a time, only 35-50% of rate gains reached EBITDA in 2024-2025, financial leverage adds little, and the main loops are balancing (orders, stored capacity) or pro-cyclical; over the four forecast years the gearing gives one year of 20% EPS on 5.5% revenue and then runs mildly backwards, so it sits just above the ordinary mix, between the groups' 56 and 28 but nearer the structural reading.

6Forecast financials, and the scope for double-digit growth

The forecasts show one contracted year of double-digit growth, then a slow decline on lower margins than the past; the improvement worth owning is in cash from 2028, not in earnings.

FY2025 EPS is the brokers’ basis. Rows after my change are my arithmetic until the model is updated.

The one change I make to the model, and why. The model of record assumes that the renewing 41% of the book reprices by about USD 18 per cbm on average. I use about USD 15, because four pieces of evidence point the same way:

1

The equipment manufacturer’s contract (USD 950m over three years, a fifth to a quarter of the renewing tranche’s revenue) is reported as renewed at rate levels similar to the previous contract. The report rests on one account of the press release, so I give it weight without leaning on it.

2

The book’s average rate did not rise (it moved from USD 55 to 54 per cbm) while 40% of volume was extended during 2026.

3

Only USD 0.8 of the USD 3 rise in the third quarter’s reported rate came from price; the rest came from cargo mix.

4

The first 2027 guidance range should centre near USD 1.80–1.85bn (#4), and outcomes have landed 0–6% below the first guidance midpoint for three years. The model’s base of 1,868 sat above its own expected guidance.

The lower renewal price removes about USD 50m of EBITDA in 2027 and USD 60m a year in 2028–2029. 2030 is unchanged, because a tranche that rose less has less to give back.

Double-digit growth comes in one year only. 2027 grows strongly; the four years from 2026 to 2030 as a whole do not.

2027 onlyEBITDA +14% · EPS +20%one contracted year of double-digit growth
2026 to 2030, a yearEBITDA +1% · EPS −1%no double-digit growth over four years

Against the past, the forecasts are weaker on every earnings line. Revenue sits on a slightly higher plateau than in 2023–2025 (USD 5.4–5.7bn against 5.1–5.3bn). EBITDA margins are two to four points below 2023–2025, because the cost base moved up in 2025–2026 and is not coming back down. EPS is below the 2023–2025 level in every forecast year.

Cash is the line that improves. Equity free cash flow roughly doubles in 2028 and reaches about USD 855m in 2029 (USD 1.94 a share, 11% of today’s price) as spending on the Shapers ends. Dividends of USD 4.25 a share over 2027–2029 (about NOK 41, a quarter of today’s price) are funded by ship loans in 2027, matched by free cash flow in 2028 and covered 1.3 times in 2029.

History shows where the peak was: reported EPS of 2.02 to 2.41 in 2023–2025, above every forecast year.

Consensus has the shape Viewforth disputes, a 2027 step then a dip in 2028 (EBITDA 1,827 to 1,679), and no 2029 yet.

Where I differ from the market. Consensus has a “V then dip” shape, with 2028 EBITDA down 8%. My forecast has a “step, hold, then ease” shape: the contracts hold 2028 and move the decline to 2029–2030. No broker yet publishes a 2029 forecast.

Strongest counter-case. The two most recent full broker updates put 2028 EBITDA near USD 1,910m, on more volume from the Shapers. If the new fleet adds capacity instead of replacing charters, revenue will be higher than I forecast.

Watch

What would change my view. The three February tests (#9), above all a book average rate of USD 60 per cbm or more.

Conclusion: the forecasts show one contracted year of double-digit growth followed by a slow decline on lower margins than the past; the improvement worth owning is in cash from 2028, not in earnings.

Score: 17, set by the Rater. Falling EPS gives F; I place it in the upper part of the band because the decline is mild and organic, with one contracted year of +20% and equity free cash flow doubling from 2028, but held well below 24 because EPS stays below 2023-2025 in every year and margins run two to four points below the past, with the 2029-2030 reset still ahead.

9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts

Earnings risk is small and trackable (about ±10% of 2027 EBITDA, halving on 17 February), but share-price risk is large, sits in the multiple and in 2029–2030, and can arrive suddenly.

Simplicity. The case is simple to state and to track: one variable (the renewal price) on one tranche (41% of the book), disclosed largely on one date. Such concentration would normally hurt predictability; here the variable is fixed by contract and soon observable.

Test 1

Book average rate (USD 54 per cbm at 30 September). A rate of about USD 60 or more supports the base case; USD 57 or less points to the low case.

Test 2

Backlog and contract duration (USD 5.8bn and 2.8 years at 30 September). Both should rise above about USD 8bn and three years if the renewal round is complete. A backlog that grew on contract length alone would show that the company again sold duration, not price.

Reported EBITDA beside adjusted EBITDA, and cash flow. Port fees would show up in the gap between reported and adjusted EBITDA and in cash flow.

Red: sudden or large; amber: gradual or medium; green: trackable or slow. The memo’s table, coloured.

Fragilities the market under-watches
Contracts fix price, not production. The chief executive says customers have “industrial optionality but not market optionality”: customers may make fewer cars, but must ship what they make with the company. He also “works with them to defer or move commitments”. The contracts are therefore firmer than the old share-of-exports contracts and softer than take-or-pay contracts.
Everything reprices at once. The three-year contracts, the HMG contract and Hyundai Glovis’s own contract with HMG all end on 31 December 2029; the first Jinling-built ships arrive in 2030; the EUKOR options open in 2031.

Sector precedent.

The give-back is slow. After the last supply wave the company’s average rate fell from USD 57 per cbm (2012) to USD 41 (2017–2018) over five to six renewal rounds.
Contracts hold price through a shock. In 2020 the rate held (USD 41.4 against 42.3 per cbm) through a 45% fall in volume, though leverage reached 6.4 times and the dividend was cancelled.
Shares peak before earnings. Shipping share prices have peaked with the ship-ordering cycle, two to four years before reported earnings.
Contract cover protects relatively, not absolutely. Container-ship lessors with backlogs equal to their whole enterprise value traded on 3–4 times earnings in 2022–2023, yet returned +27% in the first year of the downturn while container lines exposed to spot rates fell 23%.
Daily moves shared with Höegh Autoliners70%
Beta to the sector basket1.8

Share-price risk is much larger than earnings risk. Over six months, 70% of the daily variation in the shares is shared with Höegh Autoliners. A fair trough is about NOK 85–100 (roughly book value, or seven times a normal EBITDA of USD 1.0bn), and the market would price that trough six to twelve months before earnings showed the decline.

Where I differ from the market. The market is watching the right external risks (Suez, port fees, China). The market is not watching the calendar risks, which need no event to arrive.

Strongest counter-case. With 90% of volume contracted, leverage of 1.3 times and a third of the fleet returnable to its owners, Wallenius Wilhelmsen is the lowest-risk way to own the car-carrier cycle. I agree in relative terms, and that relative safety is why a de-rating of the sector would make this company the one worth looking at.

Watch

What would change my view. Disclosure of minimum volumes in the 2026 contracts; contracts longer than three years with Chinese customers; a published policy on recovering port fees from customers.

Conclusion: the forecasts are simple, concentrated and unusually trackable, with earnings risk of about ±10% for 18 months; the risk to the shares is much larger, sits in the multiple and in 2029–2030, and can be sudden on events the company does not control.

Score: 35, set by the Rater. The earnings case is simple and contract-fixed, one variable on 41% of the book, observable on 17 February, but the memo's 2027 EPS cone is about +/-20% skewed down by dated sudden steps (a full year of US port fees is -16% of EPS), ten customers are half the business, everything reprices at once at end-2029, and the share price carries a beta of 1.8 to a cyclical sector whose shares historically peak years before earnings, with a fair trough 40-48% lower; this sits between the groups' 26 and 46, below Fevertree's single-transition risk and above Storskogen's opaque conglomerate.

10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

The stock is late in its reinforcing phase: one confirming step is due in February, and stalling is the most likely phase by the second half of 2027.

Evidence.

  • The phase is still reinforcing now. Contract awards confirm the thesis, and one more confirming step is due in February.
  • Signs of the next phase, stalling, are appearing. Upgrades are running out (#7); the price is below the placement price (#8); the companies that know the market best are issuing shares and ordering ships (#5); and one of the two controlling families (Wallenius Lines) is reported not to have subscribed in the October placement, while the other was allocated 17% of the placement against a 38% holding (sources in the end notes). No insider is selling, which matters, but none is buying in size.

Stalling is therefore my central case for the end of 2027, at about 50%. The stock stays reinforcing (about 30%) only if Suez stays closed, exports hold and guidance is raised. 11The fair multiple

The guideline multiple of 7.69 times is a fair ceiling but a generous centre, and like for like the stock already pays about 9.6 times, so the guideline sits about 20% below today’s multiple.

Evidence.

  • The guideline. The guideline fair multiple is 7.69 times two-year-forward earnings: the 90th percentile of the stock’s own ten-year history (118 of 120 months), which is the band the guideline assigns to a Reinforcing phase. The other bands are 3.7x (10th percentile), 5.3x (median) and 6.5x (75th percentile).
  • Four readings of today’s multiple have one explanation. The Phases file shows 13.6x, which appears to be the September month-end reading carried forward (NOK 182.7 on that day’s consensus). Since September, consensus 2028 EPS has risen 31% and the price has fallen 11%, so FactSet’s current reading is 9.5x. The model shows 8.2x because it divides by EPS before the minority. On my EPS after the minority the multiple is about 9.6x. Like for like, the guideline is therefore about 20% below today’s multiple, not 43%.
  • How the multiple fell. The multiple fell from 13.6x to 9.5x in six weeks through upgrades, not through price. The upgrade channel is now largely spent (#7).
  • The stock’s own history. Outside the earnings collapse of 2020, the multiple was never above 8x in the ten years before 2026. In 2022–2025, when the company earned more than it will in 2027 and had a longer backlog, the market paid 3–6x.
  • Contracted shipping at earnings peaks. Container-ship lessors with full backlogs traded at 3–4x, and Japanese shipping majors at about 2x in 2021. Carriers of liquefied natural gas (LNG) on long take-or-pay charters are the exception, at 11–12x.
  • What brokers do. The most influential broker valuation is seven times a long-term EBITDA of USD 1.4bn. That long-term EBITDA input was USD 0.7bn in February 2025, 0.85bn in May 2026 and 1.0bn in August 2026.

My view: 7.69x is a fair ceiling and a generous centre.

For 7.69x: earnings are contracted to 2029; leverage is low; the yield is about 8%; forward earnings are flat for the next twelve months; and the business is sturdier than in the years that make up most of the ten-year history.
Against 7.69x: (1) a 90th-percentile multiple is normally paid for rising earnings, and the two-year-forward window is about to hold falling ones; (2) the company’s contracts run 2.8 years with volume flexibility, nearer the lessors’ kind of contract than the gas carriers’; (3) the guideline is drawn from multiples of consensus earnings after the minority, so it should be applied to EPS after the minority, whereas the model applies it to EPS before the minority (see end notes).
Net: over 18 months I would treat 6.5x to 7.7x as the fair range, with the guideline at the top. 5.3x becomes the reference if the cycle visibly turns.

Strongest counter-case. If the 2026 contracts really are firmer and longer than any before, the LNG-carrier template is the right comparison and 9–10x is fair.

Watch

What would change my view. Evidence of minimum volumes or five-year terms across the book; or a first 2029 consensus that is flat instead of down.

Conclusion: the guideline multiple of 7.69x is defensible as the top of a fair range for a late reinforcing phase but generous as its centre, and it should be read against earnings after the minority, on which today’s multiple is about 9.6x.

13Summary conclusion

Wallenius Wilhelmsen is a well-run, top-two operator doing the right things at the top of its cycle: selling three years of capacity while customers will pay for security, renewing its fleet with ships ordered cheaply, and paying out most of what it earns. Those actions make 2027 and 2028 earnings among the most predictable in shipping, and they make the dividend dependable: about 8% a year, and a quarter of the share price over three years.

These facts are known to everyone, and they are in a share price that has doubled. Guidance has no cushion, consensus estimates for 2027 already equal mine, and the multiple is above the top of its ten-year range. What is not in the narrative is mostly unhelpful and arrives by the calendar: EPS and cash run below what EBITDA suggests, and the whole contract book reprices at the end of 2029. What the share price really depends on is a “normal” level of earnings for the 2030s; the leading broker has doubled that normal level in under two years, and no report can test it before the 2030s arrive.

The verdict

The case today is one of delivery without surprise: a good yield attached to a likely de-rating, not the skew of fundamental outcomes and upgrades that Richard looks for. The stock is worth keeping close, for a constructive reason. If the car-carrier trade de-rates on a Suez or China headline while the February report confirms the contracts, the company’s contracted cash would be on offer at a normal multiple. That combination, not today’s set-up, is where the skew would turn positive. The dates to work from are 9 January, 17 February and 1 April 2027.

43

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 43, set by the Rater. The input forces are mildly positive (external 55, internal 54) and reach profits surely but only once, a contracted 2027 step of about +20% in EPS, while the financial outputs fail the test, EPS falling about 1% a year over four years to below the 2023-2025 level with margins below the past, so the net change is a mild negative that sits in the low 40s.

49

Foundations' Robustness: 49, set by the Rater. A top-two, contract-backed franchise with sticky integrated customers, low leverage and an honest operator (quality 52) is offset by scarcity-only pricing power, through-cycle returns below the cost of capital and a delivery record of meeting EBITDA and missing a little below it with no raises (guidance and delivery 40), so the foundations are sound but typical.

18

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 18, set by the Rater. In substance the case is the mirror of a quality cyclical at trough (peak earnings in a cyclical industry), and as a Demand-driven EPS Upgrader its step-up lasts one year, stays below the previous peak and reverses by 2030, so the best-fitting setup lacks its central element of sustained upgrade; set on fit alone, without counting that the step is already in estimates, this is a weak fit just above the inverse cases.

40

Case Riskiness: 40, set by the Rater. Like Richard's Arteche, the operating case is simple and the main risk of a large fall is a record multiple on a sentiment-driven sector trade, but here the earnings themselves carry dated sudden steps (port fees, policy dates), a +/-20% EPS cone, a single 2029 repricing cliff and a cyclical sector whose shares peak before earnings, with a fair trough 40-48% lower, so it sits well below 60 though above the riskiness score of 35 because leverage of 1.3 times and contracts to 2029 rule out a balance-sheet outcome.

End notes

Bases used throughout. “EBITDA” is the company’s adjusted EBITDA, which is the brokers’ basis. “EPS” is after the 20% of EUKOR Car Carriers owned by Hyundai Motor Group (HMG), which is what brokers forecast and shareholders receive; where the memo writes “as the model shows it”, the figure is before that minority and about 10% higher. “cbm” is cubic metres of cargo space, the unit in which the company prices its contracts.

Forecasts. The forecasts are the Financial Analyst’s model (update 2) with the one change of judgement made and explained in #6: a lower renewal price, entered as revenue growth and EBITDA margin and recorded in inputs-changed.md.

Latest results. The latest Earnings Review covers the quarter to 30 September 2026: the report was published on 4 November 2026, and its revenue (1,401) and EPS (0.45) match FactSet’s third quarter, so the memo relies on it.

October placement (#10). Earlier research had the second controlling family taking its full share of the placement; the placement announcements cited in the newer research give it 2.85m of the 17.15m shares, which the memo uses.

Open point with the Financial Analyst (#11, #12). The model applies the guideline multiple to EPS before the minority; the guideline is drawn from earnings after the minority, so the like-for-like figures in #11 and #12 apply it after the minority.

Charts and tables. The default charts and tables come from the visuals built from the Financial Analyst’s model (update 3) and FactSet; each carries its own note. The tables headed by FactSet figures use FactSet’s reported basis, which differs from the company’s adjusted EBITDA used in the text.

Charts drawn for this page (timeline, EBITDA to earnings, cash against dividend, judgements, range of 2027 EBITDA, brokers, return by multiple, ‘normal’ EBITDA, multiple readings, logistics margin, EBITDA against EPS, return by basis) take their figures from the memo; where a figure is Viewforth’s own arithmetic on the memo’s numbers, its note says so.

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
